haiku-low.q1: Neither. Cursors go from the gateway to Redis (caret hash and pub/sub). Postgres loses only the presence table, and the document service is untouched.
haiku-low.q2: At most one cursor per 50 ms per connection. The gateway silently drops faster ones. The client keeps the latest pending caret and sends it when the window opens.
haiku-low.q3: It holds the caret, keeping only the highest-seq held caret per user, and draws it once appliedRev reaches that caret's revision.
haiku-low.q4: If at or below appliedRev, it transforms the position forward to appliedRev. If the old revision is gone (HistoryGone, beyond the last 500), it drops the position and hides the caret until the user's next update.
haiku-low.q5: One caret and one presence entry per user, deduplicated by userId. The user stays listed until the lease on their last connection ends, or disappears at once on a clean close.
haiku-low.q6: Clean close: well under 2 s, since the closing node runs ZREM and PUBLISH at once. Node crash: worst case 40 s, inside the 45 s budget.
haiku-low.q7: Redis. Membership is a sorted set per doc, one member per connection. Identity is a hash per connection, and the caret is a hash per user. Heartbeats every 10 s extend leases and TTLs.
haiku-low.q8: A surviving node with local sockets on the doc sweeps the sorted set every 10 s and ZREMs expired members. The node whose ZREM returns 1 publishes a leave hint, and clients re-read on it.
haiku-low.q9: An accepted cursor is published on the cursor channel. Receiving nodes apply the seq and revision rules, then send it to their clients. Same-node viewers: NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q10: Joins read the full current state from Redis, not pub/sub history, so no join is missed. Missed cursor messages are corrected by the next move. A leave during loading: NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q11: The newcomer's snapshot includes each user's last caret from Redis. Every client sends an initial cursor on open, and heartbeats keep local users' carets alive, so idle users keep their caret.
haiku-low.q12: It drops any caret whose seq is not above the last seq shown for that user. Seq is per user and ordered across that user's tabs.

sonnet.q1: No. The document says the edit path and document service are untouched. Cursor state lives in Redis (caret hash plus pub/sub). Postgres only loses the presence table. It never says cursors go through the document service.
sonnet.q2: The gateway accepts at most one cursor per 50 ms per connection. It silently drops any that come faster, and they never reach Redis. The client must keep the latest pending caret and send it when the window opens.
sonnet.q3: It holds it and does not draw it. For each user it keeps only the held caret with the highest seq. It draws it when appliedRev reaches that rev.
sonnet.q4: If rev is at or below appliedRev, the client calls transformPosition(pos, rev, appliedRev) and draws the result. If it throws HistoryGone (rev older than the last 500 kept), the client drops the position and hides that caret until the user's next update.
sonnet.q5: The snapshot is deduplicated by userId, so the user appears once. They stay listed until the lease on their last connection ends. (There is one caret and one seq per user.)
sonnet.q6: Clean tab close: well under the 2 s budget. Node death: within the 45 s budget. The worst case is 40 s (30 s lease plus a sweep of up to 10 s).
sonnet.q7: In Redis. Membership is a sorted set per document, with one member per connection (connId) and the lease deadline as score. Identity is a hash per connection. Carets are a hash per user per document (seq, pos, rev). The owning node's heartbeat every 10 s extends the leases, TTLs and caret TTL. Every key has a TTL (30 s for conn and caret, 60 s for the set).
sonnet.q8: The entries expire on their own, because nothing refreshes them. The conn and caret hashes expire by TTL. Any surviving node with local sockets on the doc sweeps the sorted set every 10 s and ZREMs expired members. Only the node whose ZREM returns 1 publishes the leave hint, which tells the other nodes to re-read. They then send clients a new snapshot.
sonnet.q9: The accepted cursor is written to Redis (HINCRBY, HSET, PEXPIRE) and PUBLISHed on the doc's cursor channel. Nodes subscribed to that channel receive it, and it reaches viewers on other nodes that way. How a viewer on the sender's own node receives it is NOT STATED.
sonnet.q10: The joining node first subscribes to the channels, then writes its membership. It then reads the full current state from Redis (ZRANGEBYSCORE, HMGET, HGETALL), not from pub/sub history, and sends that snapshot. The document says no join is missed this way. It does not describe handling a leave or cursor message that arrives during the load. Missed cursors are harmless because the next move corrects them.
sonnet.q11: The last caret of each user is stored in the Redis caret hash. The join snapshot includes it. Every client sends an initial cursor on open, so even an idle user has a caret stored. The heartbeat refreshes the caret TTL for local users, so an idle user keeps it.
sonnet.q12: With seq, a per-user counter that goes up on every accepted caret update. The client drops any caret whose seq is not above the last seq shown for that user.
